title: Verifier‑Assisted versus LLM‑Only Pre‑deployment Network‑Change Validation: A Preregistered Paired Study
abstract: We measured whether integrating a deterministic pre‑deployment verifier with a bounded automated repair budget increases the fraction of intent‑driven network‑change proposals that pass semantic validation compared with accepting a single LLM candidate. In a preregistered paired design (study id cnsmp2026-llm-verifier-predeployment-001) we executed 300 paired intents (100 per difficulty stratum: low/medium/high) using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic semantic validator. Each paired intent produced one shared_initial candidate reused for two conditions: baseline (accept single shot) and guarded (deterministic validation plus ≤1 automated repair). Results: baseline 299/300 unflagged passes (0.996667), guarded 300/300 (1.000000); contingency n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0; absolute paired difference = 0.0033333; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% paired bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.01] (bootstrap_seed = 1729, B = 10000). Under the supplied synthetic suite and the bounded repair design the single‑shot generator was near ceiling, limiting observable deterministic rescue to one sequencing omission corrected by the permitted edit. We archive preregistration, execution, and analysis artifacts and interpret results with respect to estimand conditioning, validator coverage, repair budget, and operational deployment policies.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are rapidly being applied to network operations (NetOps) tasks such as intent→configuration translation, configuration template synthesis, automated repair, and protocol test generation. For pre‑deployment changes, semantic correctness properties—required sequencing, reachability, and policy preservation—are operationally critical and transcend purely syntactic correctness. A common engineering pattern couples a generator with deterministic validators and bounded automated repair (generate→validate→repair) to reduce risk before deployment. However, the measurable benefit of such guarded pipelines depends on what is held fixed (the estimand), single‑shot generator quality, validator expressiveness, and the permitted repair budget.

We preregistered and executed a paired experiment (study id cnsmp2026-llm-verifier-predeployment-001) that isolates the deterministic rescue attainable when the same single LLM draw is evaluated under two treatments. For each intent the pipeline produced exactly one shared_initial candidate using the declared generator (gpt-5-mini) and compared: (a) baseline—accept the single candidate without repair; and (b) guarded—run a deterministic validator and allow at most one automated repair, with deterministic re‑validation of any repaired candidate. Our primary research question: does adding a deterministic verifier plus at most one automated repair increase the probability that a single LLM candidate passes semantic pre‑deployment validation compared with accepting that same candidate without repair?

Contributions: (1) a preregistered paired evaluation that conditions on a single LLM draw per intent to bound deterministic rescue; (2) a complete artifact bundle (preregistration, task manifests, validator traces, repair transcript, and analysis) enabling deterministic replay; and (3) an evidence‑grounded interpretation of ceiling effects, estimand choices, validator coverage, and operational implications for NetOps CI/CD policies.
sections.related_work:
Recent surveys and system papers document progressive application of LLMs to NetOps tasks (intent translation, template synthesis, test generation, and repair) and emphasize architectural tradeoffs in tool augmentation and verification [1–4]. Planner‑centric and ReAct‑style tool‑augmented frameworks allow models to call external validators or simulators to decompose complex workflows and coordinate multi‑step changes [2,5]. Empirical work shows that introducing deterministic checks and generate→validate→repair scaffolds often improves correctness metrics relative to unconstrained generation, but reported gains depend heavily on validator coverage, task distributions, and whether pipelines permit resampling or verifier‑guided regeneration [3,1].

Two methodological themes motivated our design. First, prior evaluations frequently conflate benefits from deterministic validation with benefits from resampling or interactive regeneration; disentangling these sources requires explicitly defined estimands [3,6]. Second, many public NetOps benchmarks emphasize syntactic or template correctness rather than semantically rich invariants (sequencing, reachability, policy preservation), limiting operational generality [7,8]. Work proposing verifier‑centric benchmarks calls for validators that can express sequencing and reachability constraints, but broad community adoption remains incomplete [7]. Our study addresses these gaps by measuring bounded deterministic rescue under a shared_initial estimand that prevents resampling benefits and by evaluating semantic validation outcomes tied to explicit sequencing and preservation invariants.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. The full confirmatory design was preregistered (study id cnsmp2026-llm-verifier-predeployment-001). The primary estimand is the absolute paired difference in the unflagged verifier‑pass proportion (guarded − baseline) on N = 300 paired intents after applying predeclared inclusion/exclusion rules. The preregistration fixed the primary analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1), the use of an exact two‑sided McNemar test for discordant counts, and a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI with seed = 1729 and B = 10000.

Task generation and stratification. Tasks were generated deterministically into a synthetic topology suite stratified into three difficulty strata (low/medium/high). Each task encodes: (i) the natural‑language intent, (ii) initial and expected final device states, (iii) required sequencing constraints (e.g., must_be_down_for_fields), (iv) preserve_unspecified_state invariants, and (v) protected_interfaces. Difficulty metadata (changed_interface_count, dependency_rule_count, required_command_count) determined stratum membership; the confirmatory run sampled 100 pairs per stratum.

Shared_initial protocol and model configuration. To isolate deterministic verifier/repair effects from resampling, we implemented a shared_initial estimand: for each pair a single LLM candidate was generated and reused verbatim for both baseline and guarded conditions. The declared generator was gpt-5-mini (requested_model recorded in execution metadata). Reusing one candidate across conditions prevents outcome differences due to independent additional model draws and ensures measured differences reflect only deterministic validation and bounded repair applied to the identical output.

Deterministic validator and repair operator. Semantic evaluation used a deterministic netops validator that implements a full_intent_constraint_validation rule set: sequencing invariants, required_command_count checks, preservation of unspecified state, topology reachability invariants encoded by the suite, and protections for guarded interfaces. Scoring is binary: an unflagged candidate is a pass. The guarded pipeline permitted at most one automated repair attempt per pair (repair budget ≤ 1). The repair operator is a constrained edit routine limited to localized sequencing or insertion edits (for example, inserting a missing 'admin down' before a VLAN/MTU change). Repairs are applied only when the validator flags the shared_initial candidate and are deterministically re‑validated; repaired candidates that remain flagged count as failures for the guarded condition.

Contamination, exclusions, and execution constraints. The preregistration required one intentionally broken negative control per stratum and deterministic contamination detection. Pairs were excluded from confirmatory analysis only if both pipeline calls for that pair failed due to provider/infrastructure outage; single‑call failures were handled per executor rules with a planned sensitivity analysis treating single failures as failures when appropriate. The run respected a maximum model‑call budget and the repair budget; in practice no dual‑call outages occurred and no pairs were excluded.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. The adapter completed all planned episodes: completed_episode_count = 600 yielding complete_pair_count = 300 under the shared_initial protocol. Total model calls used = 301 (300 shared_initial generations + 1 repair invocation). No provider or infrastructure outages required exclusions; missingness was zero.

Primary confirmatory outcomes. Binary scoring produced baseline_success_count = 299 and guarded_success_count = 300 (baseline rate = 0.9966667, guarded rate = 1.0). The paired contingency table is n11 = 299, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The absolute paired improvement (guarded − baseline) equals 0.0033333. The preregistered exact two‑sided McNemar test operating on the discordant counts returned p = 1.0. The paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (seed = 1729, B = 10000) is [0.00, 0.01]. Because discordance is minimal (m = 1), the exact test has limited sensitivity; the bootstrap CI bounds the plausible absolute improvement to at most one percentage point in this experimental context.

Per‑stratum diagnostics and repair trace. Per the difficulty taxonomy, per‑stratum tallies were: low baseline = 100/100 and guarded = 100/100; medium baseline = 100/100 and guarded = 100/100; high baseline = 99/100 and guarded = 100/100. The single discordant pair occurred in the high stratum and invoked the permitted automated repair. Validator traces attribute the initial failure to a sequencing omission (the required 'admin down' prior to a VLAN/MTU change was missing). The constrained edit repair inserted the missing sequencing command; re‑validation reported valid == true. Thus the guarded pipeline produced one deterministic rescue at the cost of a single additional repair stage call.

Contamination and negative controls. Preplanned contamination checks and negative controls raised no anomalies in the confirmatory run. Contamination summary and missingness diagnostics were empty; all determinism and reconciliation checks passed.

Operational footprint. The guarded pipeline required one extra model/repair stage across 300 pairs (model_calls_used = 301, repair_stage_count = 1), indicating that, for this synthetic suite and confined repair operator, bounded deterministic rescue imposes minimal additional model‑call cost.
sections.discussion:
Estimand conditioning and operational alignment. The shared_initial estimand corresponds to operational policies that limit model calls per change request (cost, latency, governance). Under such policies the guarded pipeline measures only deterministic validator and bounded repair rescue applied to the same candidate. Workflows that permit resampling or verifier‑guided regeneration change the estimand and typically increase success rates by exploiting generator variance; those workflows require separate preregistered evaluations.

Ceiling effects and power. The preregistration planned a pilot for discordance estimation and power calibration; that pilot was not executed. The main run encountered a near‑ceiling baseline (299/300), producing minimal discordance (m = 1) and limited power to detect small absolute differences. This outcome highlights the practical benefit of small calibration pilots when generator performance may approach ceiling on chosen task suites.

Validator coverage and failure‑mode dependence. The observed failure mode was a sequencing omission; other classes (reachability violations, forbidden ACL removal) were not encountered at scale on this synthetic suite. The marginal utility of a guarded pipeline therefore depends on (a) the deployment distribution of failure modes and (b) validator expressiveness: richer validators able to check reachability or complex ACL semantics may increase rescue rates.

Repair budget tradeoffs. We intentionally limited automated repair to a single constrained edit to measure bounded deterministic rescue. Iterative repair, larger edit operators, or interactive verifier‑guided generation would increase rescue opportunities but address a different estimand and would incur higher model‑call cost. Our archived repair trace documents the localized edit that produced the single rescue and can inform choices about permitted edit operators in production policies.

Practical implications for NetOps CI/CD. Organizations should align evaluation estimands with operational choices: (i) if pipelines permit multiple model calls or verifier‑guided regeneration, evaluations should permit resampling to measure achievable success rates under that policy; (ii) if model calls are tightly budgeted, the shared_initial estimand provides an operationally meaningful bound for deterministic verifier/repair rescue applied to a single candidate. In this run bounded repair produced measurable rescue at very low additional model cost for the single rescued episode, but the near‑ceiling baseline limits extrapolation to distributions with more frequent semantic failures.
sections.conclusion: We conducted a preregistered, artifact‑archived paired comparison between a verifier‑assisted pipeline (deterministic validator + ≤1 automated repair) and accepting a single‑shot LLM candidate under the shared_initial estimand on 300 synthetic NetOps intents using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic validator. Baseline single‑shot generation produced 299/300 unflagged verifier passes and the guarded pipeline 300/300, yielding an absolute paired improvement of 0.0033333 (exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI [0.00,0.01]). The single deterministic rescue corrected a sequencing omission via one constrained edit. The near‑ceiling baseline constrains inferential sensitivity to small absolute improvements under the shared_initial estimand. We release full preregistration, execution, and analysis artifacts to enable reproducibility and targeted follow‑ups that vary estimand conditioning, model strength, task distributions, or repair budgets.

limitations: Synthetic benchmark: tasks and topologies were generated deterministically; real‑world heterogeneity may expose different failure modes and increase verifier marginal utility.
Single model and validator: only gpt-5-mini and the declared deterministic validator were evaluated; results may not generalize to other LLMs or richer/diverse validators.
Ceiling effect: baseline single‑shot performance was near 100% on this suite (299/300), producing limited discordance and reduced power to detect small absolute improvements.
Pilot not executed: the preregistered pilot intended for discordance estimation and power calibration was not run; no post‑preregistration power recalculation was performed.

Estimand conditioning: the shared_initial protocol conditions the estimand on a single LLM candidate and therefore does not measure verifier benefit that would arise from allowing independent alternative LLM candidates per condition (resampling or iterative generation).
Repair budget: the guarded condition permitted at most one automated repair per pair; larger or iterative repair strategies may yield different outcomes.
